detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?
detail.answer:
Mill claims that women who have ruled have shown real ability, and that the record counts in favour of women's capacity for government. His main points are:

- Reigning queens are few compared with kings, but a far larger proportion of them have shown talents for rule, often in difficult periods. They have been noted for firmness and vigour as much as for intelligence. Adding regents and viceroys of provinces, the list of eminent women rulers grows very long. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific))
- Mill says it is certain, as a matter of fact and not inference, that a woman can be a Queen Elizabeth, a Deborah, or a Joan of Arc. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific))
- In a footnote he cites his own official knowledge of Hindoo governments. He says that in three cases out of four, a well-governed Hindoo principality is under a woman's rule. A woman cannot reign there, but she is the legal regent during an heir's minority. He calls this a very striking example of women's natural capacity for government, since these princesses were secluded and had no political education. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific))
- He answers the joke that under kings women govern but under queens men govern. Two princesses who governed the Netherlands for Charles the Fifth ruled very successfully, and one of them, Margaret of Austria, was among the ablest politicians of her age. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific))
- He argues that most great queens were great through their own talents for government. They kept the supreme direction of affairs in their own hands, and when they took good advice, that showed good judgment. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific))
- He concludes that wherever and to the extent that women's capacities for government have been tried, they have been found adequate. He attributes this to princesses having been allowed the same range of interests and freedom of development as men. (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific))

detail.answer: Kant treats the understanding as the faculty that does the combining. The senses can give the manifold (the diverse content) of intuition, but never its conjunction. Conjunction is a spontaneous act of the faculty of representation, and that faculty, distinguished from sensibility, is called the understanding. So every conjunction, whether of the manifold in intuition or of several conceptions, conscious or unconscious, is an act of the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §11, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Kant calls this act synthesis: joining different representations to each other and comprehending their diversity in one cognition. He calls it the first requisite for producing cognition (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Because we cannot represent anything as conjoined in the object without having conjoined it ourselves, the combining originates in the subject. Analysis presupposes it, since the understanding cannot dissect what it has not first conjoined (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §11, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The understanding also supplies unity: the same function that unifies representations in a judgement unifies the mere synthesis of representations in an intuition, and this unity is the pure conception of the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Within the three requisites Kant lists for cognition of an object, the manifold of pure intuition comes first and its synthesis by imagination second, but that synthesis gives no cognition yet. The conceptions that give unity to this pure synthesis are given by the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). Finally, all union of representations requires unity of consciousness in their synthesis (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §13, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Kant says the synthetical unity of apperception is the highest point to which every operation of the understanding must be connected, and that this faculty is the understanding itself (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Note block 155 to Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What criticism does Hume make of philosophers who claim that all power belongs directly to God?
detail.answer: Hume's criticism is that these philosophers, in trying to honor God, actually diminish him. Some philosophers hold that mind is the immediate and sole cause of every event in nature. They say that what we call causes are only "occasions," and that the true principle of every effect is a volition (act of will) of the Supreme Being (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §55, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume says they go further and strip nature and all created beings of every power, so as to make their dependence on the Deity more sensible and immediate (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His objection is that they overlook how this theory lessens the grandeur of the very attributes they celebrate. He argues that it shows more power in the Deity to delegate some power to creatures than to produce everything by his own immediate volition. It also shows more wisdom to design the world at first so that it serves providence by its own operation than to have the Creator adjust its parts at every moment (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft says children should not be taught to make allowances for their parents' faults. She argues that "Children cannot, ought not to be taught to make allowance for the faults of their parents," because every such allowance weakens the force of reason in their minds and makes them more indulgent to their own faults (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She distinguishes this from adult virtue. Being severe with ourselves and forbearing to others is, she says, one of the most sublime virtues of maturity, but children should be taught only the simple virtues. If they start too early to make allowance for human passions and manners, they dull the "fine edge of the criterion" (the standard) by which they should regulate their own conduct, and they become unjust as they grow indulgent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She presents this as a dilemma for instructors: teaching virtue on any solid principle amounts to teaching children to despise their parents (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)).

The surrounding passages give related context. She gives an example of a girl who could hardly respect a mother who scolded her over the mother's badly dressed hair, asking what respect she could acquire "without doing violence to reason" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Note block 13 to Chapter 11, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). She also criticizes the "absurd duty" of obeying a parent merely for being a parent, which she says shackles the mind (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). She holds instead that a parent who sets a good example lets it work, and that it seldom fails to produce filial respect (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes lists four abuses of speech, and the first is the one by which people deceive themselves. It happens when men "register their thoughts wrong, by the inconstancy of the signification of their words." They then record as their conceptions something they never actually conceived (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). By contrast, he says the second abuse, using words metaphorically, deceives others (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

The passages also explain why the meaning of words can be unstable. Names of things that please or displease us are of inconstant signification, because people are affected differently, and one man calls wisdom what another calls fear (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Inconstant Names, paragraph 25 (edition-specific)). Hobbes adds that such names can never be true grounds of ratiocination (reasoning) (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Inconstant Names, paragraph 25 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft attacks these arguments in several ways. (1) She says that even if women are naturally weaker, it does not follow that they should work to become weaker still. She calls such arguments "an insult to common sense" and compares the "DIVINE RIGHT of husbands" to the divine right of kings, which she hopes can now be contested without danger (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 3, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). (2) She rejects the idea that a wife should feign "a sickly delicacy" to win her husband's affection. Weakness may gratify a man's pride, but a noble mind wants respect, and "Fondness is a poor substitute for friendship!" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 42 (edition-specific)). (3) She summarizes the opposing reasoning as inferring from women's lesser bodily strength that they should be weak and passive and should please their master. Her treatment of this reasoning is critical (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). (4) She argues that the writers who want to domesticate women use arguments that "weaken their bodies and cramp their minds," even though running a family and educating children require strength of body and mind. She holds that reason is necessary for performing any duty properly (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). (5) She likens such arguments to those of tyrants who crush reason while claiming to be useful. A duty not founded on reason cannot bind, and enforced subordination yields "convenient slaves" while degrading both master and dependent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Dedication, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). (6) She claims that "artificial weakness" breeds a propensity to tyrannize and to cunning. She says that if these prejudices are not fostered, women will fall into their subordinate yet respectable station (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Introduction, paragraph 15 (edition-specific)). (7) She asks whether strength of mind can come from "indolent acquiescence" or obeying through fear. Her conclusion is that if women are made rational creatures and free citizens, they will quickly become good wives and mothers, provided men do not neglect their own duties (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 12, paragraph 82 (edition-specific)). The passages qualify the claim about authority: she speaks of women's station as "subordinate, yet respectable" rather than rejecting all subordination outright.

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft's test is whether a reason can be given. She says a prejudice is "a fond obstinate persuasion, for which we can give no reason". As soon as a reason can be given for an opinion, it stops being a prejudice, even if it is still "an error in judgment" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). So an opinion can be wrong without being a prejudice. She also says opinions often began with some reason, but they turn into prejudices when they are "indolently adopted" only because age has given them a venerable look, after the original reason has ceased to be a reason or can no longer be traced (same passage).

The other passages describe how prejudices behave. People often use reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed without knowing how, rather than to root them out (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). She says she has often traced a heated opinion from a person of moderate abilities to a prejudice. Such people repeat opinions they do not fully understand and hold them obstinately (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)). She suggests heat can signal wavering: people assert opinions most hotly when they begin to doubt (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). Those who take opinions on credit, she says, are prey to prejudices and blindly submit to authority (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)).

By contrast, those who hold their position on a sound basis do not fear reason or the sifting of subjects (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 10, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). The passage says this of good and wise men who are convinced they have a right to what they insist on. The passages give the main criterion, that a reason can be given, and several signs of prejudice. They do not set out a fuller formal definition of a well-supported opinion.

detail.answer:
Smith says the difference lies in how concentrated or spread out the dependence is. When great landowners spend their rents on tenants and retainers, each one maintains all of his own tenants and retainers entirely (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Their subsistence comes from his bounty and lasts at his pleasure, so tenants at will are as dependent on him as any servant or retainer (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

When the same landowners spend on tradesmen and artificers, all of them together may maintain as many people as before, or perhaps more, because of the waste that attends rustic hospitality. Each landowner taken singly, however, contributes only a very small share to the maintenance of any one individual. A tradesman lives from the custom of a hundred or a thousand customers, so he is somewhat obliged to them all but is not absolutely dependent on any one (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not spell out the political consequences of this contrast in the same place, but they do say that the older method of spending shared the rents with at least 1000 people. The new method of consuming goods oneself let the proprietors keep everything for themselves and give up the authority that sharing had given them (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: The passages do not support this premise. Kant argues the opposite: scepticism does not give definitive answers to the problems of reason. He says the sceptical procedure 'does not present any solution of the problems of reason', but works as an exercise that awakens reason's circumspection and helps it establish its legitimate claims (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). In itself, scepticism gives no certain information about the bounds of our knowledge. It cannot settle the dispute over the rights and powers of human reason (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)). He calls scepticism 'merely a means of awakening reason from its dogmatic dreams' and rejects treating our conviction of ignorance as a settlement of reason's disputes with itself (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). Of Hume, the 'remarkably acute thinker' he criticizes, Kant says he declared the understanding limited without showing what its limits are. Hume therefore gave no determinate knowledge of the bounds of our ignorance, and his own declarations came to be doubted (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). Kant does grant scepticism some value. The transcendental dialectic 'does not favour scepticism', yet it shows the advantages of the sceptical method. Its result was no positive dogmatical addition to metaphysics but a correction of our judgements (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section VII, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Scepticism is thus a useful preparatory check on dogmatism, not a source of definitive answers.

detail.question: How does Hume explain the occurrence of unexpected outcomes in the human body?
detail.answer: Hume says that unexpected outcomes in the body do not show that nature is irregular. When symptoms of health or sickness disappoint expectation, or medicines fail to work as usual, the philosopher and physician are not surprised. They do not deny that the principles governing the animal economy (the workings of the body) are necessary and uniform (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). They treat the body as a very complicated machine with many hidden powers beyond our comprehension. It therefore often looks uncertain to us, and the irregular events that show on the outside are no proof that the laws of nature fail inside it (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). More generally, when a cause such as a medicine fails to produce its usual effect, philosophers suppose that some secret causes in the particular structure of parts have prevented the operation. Hume also notes that not all causes are joined to their usual effects with equal uniformity (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
Locke says power, as he is considering it, comes in two kinds: being able to make a change, which he calls ACTIVE power, and being able to receive a change, which he calls PASSIVE power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He leaves open whether matter lacks active power altogether, whether God is above all passive power, and whether created spirits alone have both. He says this may be "worth consideration" but declines to pursue it, since his business is how we come by the IDEA of power, not its origin (same passage).

He adds that sensible things abundantly supply ideas of passive power, because their qualities are in continual flux and so liable to further change. We also have many instances of active power, since any observed change makes the mind infer a power able to make it, as well as a possibility in the thing to receive it. He calls active power "the more proper signification of the word power" (Locke, Essay, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

However, he argues that bodies give us only an obscure idea of active power. A body at rest shows no power to move. A moving body, such as a ball struck by a billiard-stick, is more passive than active, since it only transfers motion it received and does not produce it (Locke, Essay, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). The clearer idea of the beginning of motion comes from reflection on our own minds, where by willing alone we move parts of our bodies that were at rest. He therefore says we get a clearer idea of active power from reflection on the mind's own operations than from external sensation (Locke, Essay, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). For the same reason, in §2 he directs us to God and spirits for the clearest idea of active power (Locke, Essay, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

His claim about bodies is hedged: if someone thinks impulse gives a clear idea of power, he says that serves his purpose just as well, since sensation is one way the mind gets its ideas (Locke, Essay, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Mill claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated?
detail.premise: Mill claims that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated.
detail.answer:
Mill does not claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice outraged. He raises that point as an objection to his view and rejects it. The objection says that when our sentiment of justice is outraged, we are thinking only of the individual case, not of society at large or any collective interest (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). Mill answers that it is common enough to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain, but this is "the reverse of commendable" (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). A person whose resentment is a real moral feeling first considers whether an act is blameable. Even if he does not say so to himself, he feels he is asserting a rule that benefits others as well as himself (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). Someone who regards an act solely as it affects him individually is, in Mill's words, "not consciously just" (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

This fits Mill's wider account. The raw feeling of retaliation is natural and tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever is disagreeable to us. It becomes moral only when subordinated to the social sympathies (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). Just persons resent a hurt to society even when it is not otherwise a hurt to themselves. They do not resent a hurt to themselves, however painful, unless it is of a kind society has a common interest in repressing (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). Mill also says the sentiment of justice is the animal desire to repel a hurt to oneself, widened to include all persons. Its morality comes from that widening, and its energy from the animal element (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant says we actually possess a priori synthetic cognitions, and he treats the principles of the understanding as proof of this: they "anticipate experience" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). A person who cannot comprehend how these principles are possible may doubt that they are really a priori. He cannot, however, declare them impossible or call the steps reason has taken under their guidance null (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere Kant explains why such judgements are puzzling. In a proposition like "Everything that happens has a cause," the concept of cause is not contained in the concept of what happens. Experience cannot supply the connection, because the principle asserts it with universality and necessity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction, Section IV, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He adds that the whole aim of our speculative a priori knowledge depends on such synthetic, "augmentative" propositions. Analytic judgements matter only for the clearness of concepts that a sure and extended synthesis requires (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction, Section IV, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Metaphysics, too, must contain synthetic a priori propositions, since it seeks to widen our a priori knowledge (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction, Section V, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

On reason's responsibility, Kant says that the conceptions and questions of pure reason lie not in the sphere of experience but in reason itself. Reason must therefore solve them and show them to be either valid or inadmissible (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). We may not decline these problems by appealing to the nature of things or to the limits of human faculties. Reason is the sole creator of these ideas, so it is bound to establish their validity or expose their illusory nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). He grants that doubt about dogmatical philosophy, which proceeds without criticism, is well grounded. But he denies that this means reason cannot construct a sound philosophy once a thorough critical investigation has prepared the way (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Hume evaluate the effectiveness of Cartesian universal doubt in achieving certainty?
detail.answer: Hume judges Cartesian universal doubt to be ineffective as a route to certainty. He describes it as a scepticism "antecedent to all study and philosophy" that Descartes and others recommend as a preservative against error. It would doubt all our former opinions and even our faculties, and then try to re-establish the faculties' veracity by a chain of reasoning from some original principle that could not be deceitful (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume gives two objections. First, no such original principle has a prerogative over other self-evident and convincing ones. Second, even if there were one, we could not advance beyond it except by using the very faculties we are supposed to distrust (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He concludes that, were such doubt ever attainable (he says plainly it is not), it would be entirely incurable, and no reasoning could bring us to assurance and conviction on any subject (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume does allow a qualified value to a more moderate form of this scepticism. In that form it is a necessary preparative to the study of philosophy, because it preserves impartiality in our judgements and weans the mind from prejudices. He adds that the real methods of reaching truth and a proper stability and certainty are starting from clear and self-evident principles, advancing by timorous and sure steps, and reviewing our conclusions. Progress by these means is slow and short (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). So the passages show Hume rejecting the extreme, universal doubt as a way to certainty, while accepting the moderate version only as a preparation and a discipline.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the words Just and Unjust mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions. Applied to men, they signify the conformity or inconformity of their manners (manner of life) to reason; applied to actions, they signify the conformity or inconformity to reason of particular actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called Righteous and Unrighteous, though the meaning is the same (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). So a righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistakes about things or persons. An unrighteous man does not lose his character through actions he does, or refrains from, out of fear, because his will is shaped by apparent benefit and not by justice (same passage). Justice of manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice (same passage).

Hobbes adds a further difference. The injustice of manners is a disposition or aptitude to do injury. It exists before it proceeds to act, and it does not presuppose any individual person injured. The injustice of an action, that is, injury, does presuppose an individual injured, namely the person to whom the covenant was made (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Manners, And Justice Of Actions, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Hence the injury may be received by one man while the damage falls on another. For example, if a servant fails to give money to a stranger as his master commanded, the injury is done to the master, but the damage falls on the stranger (same passage).

This connects to Hobbes's definition of action-injustice: once a covenant is made, breaking it is unjust, and injustice is defined as the not performance of covenant (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice And Injustice What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Burke suggests that his countrymen should hold up the British Constitution as an example to the French rather than take French models for improving their own. He says the French have "an invaluable treasure" in it (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)). He also credits Britain's happy situation to the whole Constitution, not to any single part, and in large part to what was left standing through earlier reviews and reformations (same passage).

Burke's main advice is to guard what they already possess. He says the people will find employment enough for a patriotic, free and independent spirit in protecting it from violation (paragraph 417). He does not rule out alteration, but says that even a change should be made in order to preserve. A great grievance should prompt any remedy, and repairs should follow the ancestors' example and be made as nearly as possible in the style of the building (paragraph 417). He urges imitating the caution of the forefathers, who acted with a sense of human ignorance and fallibility. He says: add if we please, but preserve what they left, and be satisfied to admire rather than follow "the aëronauts of France" in their desperate flights (paragraph 417).

He also wants the true principles of Britain's own domestic laws recalled and cherished. He warns that neither side of the Channel should be imposed upon by counterfeit goods passed off as British ideas but re-imported in the "newest Paris fashion of an improved liberty" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). He also says he is astonished that anyone could hold up anything in the new French Constitution as an example for Great Britain, since it is the reverse of Britain's in principle (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke says the preacher's claim, that the king is "almost the only lawful king in the world" because he alone owes his crown to the choice of his people, touches the British people directly. Foreign kings must worry about the claim for themselves, but for the British it is "a domestic interest of some moment" to examine seriously "the solidity of the only principle" on which these gentlemen accept that a king of Great Britain deserves allegiance (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 21 (edition-specific)).

Burke argues the doctrine is either nonsense or a "most unfounded, dangerous, illegal, and unconstitutional position." If a king is lawful only when he owes his crown to popular choice, and the king of Great Britain does not owe his office to any popular election, then he is no better than the other "usurpers" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He sees a tactic in this. The preachers hope their abstract principle will pass unnoticed while the British king seems exempt from it, and meanwhile their congregations grow used to it as an accepted first principle. It would lie ready as a theory for future use. The result is that the security government has through public opinion is taken away (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

Burke also points to wider consequences. If no throne is lawful unless elective, no act of the princes before the Revolution could be valid. That would call into question the whole line of kings and the statute law passed under them, including the Petition of Right and the Habeas Corpus act (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 43 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?
detail.answer:
The passages support a distinction between interference that is truly a question of liberty and interference that is not. They do not give a complete, systematic classification of trade regulation.

1. Restrictions that are not really questions of liberty. Mill says trade is a social act, so a seller's conduct comes within society's jurisdiction (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Restrictions on trade are still restraints, and he calls all restraint an evil. But they affect only the part of conduct that society is competent to restrain, and they are wrong only because they fail to produce the results intended (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Free Trade rests on grounds different from, though equally solid with, individual liberty. Questions such as preventing fraud by adulteration, or protecting workers in dangerous occupations, therefore involve liberty only in the limited sense that leaving people alone is generally better than controlling them. Mill says that controlling them for these ends is in principle undeniable (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

2. Interferences that are essentially questions of liberty. These are cases where the aim is to make a commodity impossible or difficult to obtain. His examples are the Maine Law, the prohibition of opium imports into China, and restrictions on the sale of poisons (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). The excerpt is cut off at the end of the paragraph, but Mill's last sentence says these are objectionable as infringements on the liberty of the buyer, not of the producer or seller (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. A further class outside the liberty principle. Mill reserves a large class of cases where the question is not restraining individuals but helping them. Here the question is whether government should do something for their benefit instead of leaving it to individuals or voluntary combination (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). He says objections to interference that does not infringe liberty may be of three kinds (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The first is that the thing is likely to be better done by individuals than by government. This condemns the once-common interference with the ordinary processes of industry (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The third, which he calls the most cogent, is the great evil of adding unnecessarily to government's power (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)). The second kind of objection is not in the supplied passages.

detail.answer: Kant claims that using general logic as an organon (an instrument for producing knowledge) goes wrong. Because general logic teaches nothing about the content of our cognitions, only the formal conditions of their agreement with the understanding, which are indifferent to objects, any attempt to use it to extend knowledge "must end in mere prating." Anyone could then maintain or oppose any assertion with some appearance of truth (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). He therefore warns that general logic, treated as an organon, must always be a "logic of illusion," that is, dialectical (same passage). Kant explains that the mere form of a cognition cannot supply material (objective) truth, so no one can decide anything about objects by logic alone without information obtained independently of logic. Yet the appeal of an art that gives cognitions the form of understanding, even when their content is lacking, has led general logic, properly only a canon of judgement, to be used as an organon for the actual or merely apparent production of objective assertions. He calls this a gross misapplication, and general logic in this assumed role is called dialectic (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section III, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not show Burke arguing that the paper currency will distribute power equally among citizens. He argues the opposite. He says the one certain effect of the scheme is to produce an oligarchy (rule by a few) in every one of the republics. A paper circulation not backed by real money deposited, and forced in place of the kingdom's coin, becomes the substance of its revenue and the medium of all commercial and civil dealings. It must therefore put whatever power, authority and influence remains into the hands of the managers and conductors of the circulation (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 331 (edition-specific)).

The closest the passages come to "equality" is Burke's account of the Assembly's motive. He says it was necessary to "put every individual on the same bottom" and to bind the nation in one guilty interest to uphold the confiscation of Church property. To force even the reluctant into sharing in the pillage, the Assembly made its paper circulation compulsory in all payments (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 220 (edition-specific)). This describes a shared stake in the confiscation, imposed by compulsion, and not an equal distribution of power. Burke also calls the compulsory paper currency a violent outrage upon credit, property and liberty (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 221 (edition-specific)).

So the question's premise is not supported by these passages. Burke presents the scheme as concentrating power in the hands of those who manage the paper.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.
detail.answer:
No. Mill separates two cases. A person who is merely imprudent or lacks personal dignity may lose others' consideration, but that is not a reason to punish him. Others may show distaste and keep their distance, but they need not make his life uncomfortable. They should reflect that he already bears the penalty of his error, so instead of punishing him they should try to ease it (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Punishment in the strict sense is reserved for someone who infringes the rules protecting others. In that case society 'must inflict pain on him for the express purpose of punishment' (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

Mill adds that a self-regarding fault becomes punishable only when it breaches a distinct duty. A man ruined by extravagance may be justly punished for failing his family or creditors, not for the extravagance itself (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Likewise, no one should be punished simply for being drunk, though a soldier or policeman drunk on duty should be (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Where conduct harms no one but the agent, Mill says society can afford to bear the inconvenience for the sake of human freedom (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). He also warns that coercing people into prudence will provoke rebellion in those of vigorous and independent character (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). In Chapter 5 he says idleness, in the ordinary case, cannot without tyranny be legally punished (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

There are qualifications. A person who has once committed violence while drunk may legitimately be placed under a special restriction. Someone who fails his legal duties to others, such as supporting his children, may be compelled to fulfil them (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). In those cases the punishment answers harm or duty to others, not the personal failing as such.

detail.answer:
Smith describes the discovery of the American mines as lowering the value of gold and silver in Europe, though he is cautious about how long the decline continued.

Relative value: Before the discovery, an ounce of fine gold was worth about 10 to 12 ounces of fine silver in the European mines. By about the middle of the last century, it was worth about 14 to 15 ounces. Smith says gold rose in its nominal value, meaning the quantity of silver given for it (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

Real value: He says both metals sank in real value, meaning the quantity of labour they could purchase, but silver sank more than gold. He explains this by saying that the silver mines of America seem to have been proportionally even more fertile than the gold ones (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere he states plainly that the discovery diminished the value of gold and silver in Europe (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Timing and cause: In the case of silver measured against corn, Smith says the discovery seems to have been the sole cause of the fall in its value. Demand was rising as Europe advanced, but supply seems to have increased so much faster that the metal's value sank considerably. He notes that the discovery had no very sensible effect on English prices until after 1570 (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)). He places the completion of the effect on silver's value, relative to corn, between 1630 and 1640. After that, silver seems never to have sunk lower, and it seems to have risen somewhat since (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53 (edition-specific)).

The ongoing decline is uncertain. In Book I he says it is commonly supposed that the diminution still goes on, but he adds that he apprehends this is without any certain proof (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). In Book IV he again says it is supposed, perhaps without much foundation, that the metals have been gradually sinking in value because of continual imports from the Spanish West Indies (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 1, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)).

Consequences: He argues that this fall in silver's value, which affects most of the commercial world about equally, matters little to any single country. Money prices rise, but this does not make those who receive them really richer or poorer. A service of plate becomes really cheaper, and everything else keeps the same real value (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft's fullest account is in Chapter 1. She says that in the "infancy of society," when men were just emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests had "unbounded sway" because they touched the most powerful springs of savage conduct, hope and fear (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She calls aristocracy "naturally the first form of government." Then, as clashing interests lost their balance ("equipoise"), a monarchy and hierarchy "break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles," and feudal tenures secure the foundation of both. She presents this as "the origin of monarchial and priestly power, and the dawn of civilization" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

She adds that this arrangement could not stay contained. Foreign wars and internal insurrections gave the people some power, which forced rulers to cover their oppression with "a show of right." As wars, agriculture, commerce and literature expanded the mind, despots had to rely on "covert corruption" instead of open force, and luxury and superstition spread this corruption most quickly (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

The other passages do not describe this early development. They only criticize later effects of monarchy and hereditary honours, such as wretchedness (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith's argument is that the bounty (a payment to exporters of corn) made some limits on importing foreign corn unavoidable. He says the restraints on importation were first imposed before the bounty and arose from the same spirit and principles. Even so, "these, or some other restraints upon importation, became necessary in consequence of that regulation," however hurtful in themselves (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 5, paragraph 78 (edition-specific)).

His reasoning is as follows. If foreign corn could come in duty free, or with only a small duty, when wheat was at or near 48s. the quarter, it could be exported again and collect the bounty. That would cost the public revenue heavily and wholly pervert the institution, whose object was to extend the market for home-grown corn, not for the growth of foreign countries (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 5, paragraph 78 (edition-specific)).

The passages say little else directly on this point. Elsewhere Smith notes that the bounty brings greater exportation in years of plenty, and so greater importation in years of scarcity than would otherwise occur (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 2, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)). He does not, however, present this as the reason for the restraints.

detail.question: What does Locke argue about the relationship between conquest and the establishment of government?
detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a source of government; legitimate government rests on the consent of the people. He says governments originally arise only from consent and that polities are founded on nothing else. People have mistaken "the force of arms for the consent of the people" because the noise of war drowns out consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His central image is that conquest is as far from setting up a government as demolishing a house is from building a new one. Conquest may make way for a new commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Locke also limits what a conqueror gains, even in a just war:
- He gets no power over those who fought alongside him, who remain freemen. Locke applies this to the Normans who came with William, arguing that even if William's conquest was rightful, it reached only the Saxons and Britons then living in the country (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).
- In a just war, the conqueror has despotical power over the lives of those who forfeited them by entering a state of war, but not a right to their possessions. Locke admits this will seem strange because it runs against the practice of the world, but he says the practice of the powerful is seldom the rule of right (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §180, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).
- Even in a just war, he has no right of dominion over those who joined him, over those of the subdued country who did not oppose him, or over the posterity of those who did. If their former government is dissolved, they are at liberty to erect another (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §185, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).
- Harm suffered in the state of nature cannot let a conqueror dispossess the descendants of the vanquished. Otherwise his claim would be only what bare force gives the stronger over the weaker, so that whoever is strongest would have a right to whatever he seizes (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
- Whoever conquers in an unjust war has no title to the subjection and obedience of the conquered (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §176, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).
- A conqueror's government imposed by force on those against whom he had no right of war, or who did not join the war against him where he had that right, has no obligation upon them (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §187, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)).
- Even if a conqueror in a just war had a right to the conquered people's estates, absolute power would not follow. Their descendants are freemen, and whatever estates he grants them become their property, which cannot be taken without their own consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).

In Chapter 4, Wollstonecraft says that when treating of education or manners, "minds of a superior class are not to be considered" and "may be left to chance". So her argument is close to the reverse of the question's premise. Superior minds can be left to chance, and it is ordinary people who most need instruction. She says that men and women of this multitude should not have their sensations heightened in the hot-bed of luxurious indolence at the expense of their understanding. detail.question: According to Hume, what distinguishes belief from mere imagination or fiction?
detail.answer: Hume says the difference is not in the ideas themselves but in a feeling that goes with belief. The imagination can combine ideas freely and can picture a fiction "with all the appearance of reality", yet some fictions still cannot be believed. We can join a man's head to a horse's body in conception, but we cannot believe such an animal ever existed (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Belief is not a special idea added to a conception, because the mind could then add it to any fiction at will and believe whatever it pleased, which daily experience contradicts (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Instead, the difference lies in a sentiment or feeling attached to belief and not to fiction. This feeling does not depend on the will and cannot be commanded at pleasure. It is excited by nature, when an object present to the memory or senses carries the imagination by custom to conceive its usual companion (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Without this sentiment there would be no difference between a conception we assent to and one we reject, since we can conceive the contrary of any matter of fact. Hume's example is the billiard-ball: we can conceive it stopping on contact, but that conception feels very different from the one in which motion passes from one ball to the other (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Hume says he cannot define this feeling perfectly, and that a definition may be difficult or even impossible. He offers a description instead: belief is a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object than the imagination alone can attain. It makes realities weigh more in thought and gives them a superior influence on the passions and imagination. Since imagination cannot of itself reach belief, belief lies not in the nature or order of the ideas but in the manner of their conception and their feeling to the mind (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). In philosophy, he says, we can go no further than to assert that belief is something felt by the mind that distinguishes the ideas of the judgement from the fictions of the imagination. It gives these ideas more weight and influence and makes them the governing principle of our actions (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He sums up the doctrine as a conception more intense and steady than what attends mere fictions, arising from a customary conjunction of the object with something present to the memory or senses (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith says wages vary more from place to place than the price of provisions does. Bread and butchers' meat cost the same or nearly the same through most of the united kingdom. Most things sold by retail are as cheap or cheaper in great towns than in remote parts, for reasons he promises to explain later. Yet wages in a great town and its neighbourhood are often 20 or 25 per cent higher than a few miles away. His examples: about eighteen pence a day in London, falling to fourteen or fifteen pence a few miles off; tenpence in Edinburgh, falling to eightpence nearby (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). He argues that if such differences do not always move a man from one parish to another, then the labouring poor must be in affluence where wages are highest, if they can maintain families where wages are lowest (same passage).

Smith does not conclude that provisions have no effect on wages. Wage changes do not always match provision-price changes and are often opposite to them. Even so, the money price of labour is regulated by two things: the demand for labour and the price of necessaries and conveniences of life. So wages may be high where provisions are cheap, but would be higher still if provisions were dear and demand were unchanged (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)).

On sharp local wage differences in England, Smith says they are "probably" caused by the law of settlements. detail.answer:
Burke thinks the ministers' position is both difficult and degrading for several reasons drawn from two passages.

1. They lack real power and are stuck between two authorities. Burke says they are "to execute, without power; they are to be responsible, without discretion; they are to deliberate, without choice." Placed "under two sovereigns" (the king and the Assembly), neither of whom they influence, they must sometimes betray one and sometimes the other, and always betray themselves (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

2. They have no confidence from either side, and their functions are taken over. They were forced on the king by the Assembly. The "noble functions of their office" are carried out by committees of the Assembly, with no regard for the ministers' personal or official authority. Burke calls this a "species of subordinate servitude" never seen before (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

3. They must witness their country's degradation. Burke says they could not help seeing and feeling the evils produced by the Revolution, and their "utter incapacity of serving" the country, from an "eminence of humiliation" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)). He says he would not have stood in their situation for the universe, and is astonished they have not resigned long since (same passage).

4. The office offers peril, not glory. In other countries the office of minister is of the highest dignity, but in France it is "full of peril, and incapable of glory." Rivals, enabled by the Constitution, can attack ministers in their vital parts, while ministers can answer only in the "degrading character of culprits." They are also the only people in France incapable of a share in the national councils (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

5. Responsibility is a poor substitute for active service. Burke grants that responsibility prevents crimes, but says it cannot inspire "active and zealous service" or make a nation glorious (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)). He also argues that if the king names the ministers they will sympathize with him, but if they are forced on him, the relationship will be mutual counteraction (same passage).

detail.answer: Locke says that the person who thinks for himself finds real satisfaction in the search for truth. The understanding, "like the eye," judges objects by its own sight and so is pleased with what it discovers. It also has less regret for what escaped it, because that is unknown (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He contrasts the person who has raised himself "above the alms-basket" with one who lives lazily on "scraps of begged opinions". The first sets his own thoughts to work to find and follow truth, and whatever he lights on, he will not miss "the hunter's satisfaction". Every moment of the pursuit rewards his pains with some delight. He has reason to think his time well spent even when he cannot boast of any great acquisition (same passage). Locke also says that in the sciences, a person has only as much as he really knows and comprehends. What he merely believes and takes on trust amounts to "shreds", which add little to his stock, and such borrowed wealth is like fairy money that turns to leaves and dust when used (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book I, Chapter 4, §24, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
Smith says the method of collection makes a large difference to how much of what the people pay actually reaches the crown. Most of France's revenue comes from eight sources: the taille, the capitation, the two vingtiemes, the gabelles, the aides, the traites, the domaine and the farm of tobacco. The last five are mostly under "farm" (collected by private contractors), while the first three are levied by an administration under the direct inspection and direction of government. It is universally acknowledged that, in proportion to what they take from the people, the government-run taxes bring more into the prince's treasury than the farmed ones, whose administration is much more wasteful and expensive (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 205 (edition-specific)).

Smith also treats the French system as a whole as inefficient. In 1765 and 1766 the revenue paid into the treasury was between 308 and 325 millions of livres, under fifteen millions sterling. That was less than half of what might have been expected if the French had contributed in proportion to their numbers as the British do. He admits his accounts of this are very imperfect. Yet the French are generally acknowledged to be much more oppressed by taxes than the British (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 207 (edition-specific)).

He suggests three reforms. First, abolish the taille and capitation and increase the vingtiemes to make up the revenue. This would preserve the crown's revenue, greatly reduce the expense of collection, and prevent the vexation of the lower ranks. Second, make the gabelle, aides, traites, tobacco taxes, customs and excises uniform across the kingdom, so that they could be levied at much less expense. Third, put all these taxes under an administration directly overseen by government (the passage breaks off mid-sentence). Smith expects the interest and opposition of favoured subjects to be the most likely obstacle to such reforms (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 206 (edition-specific)).

The provided passages also describe the way the taille is assessed. The council's yearly apportionment cannot be made with tolerable exactness. Ignorance and misinformation mislead it, and assessors are said to be swayed by friendship, party animosity and private resentment, so no one can be certain what he will owe (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 86 (edition-specific)). detail.question: Why does Locke argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies?
detail.premise: Locke holds that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies.
detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match these passages. Locke does not argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies. He argues the reverse: that private property can arise legitimately, even from a world given to everyone in common.

He starts from the idea that God gave the earth to mankind in common, and he treats this as raising a difficulty about how anyone could come to own anything (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His answer is that labour gives a title. God gave the world to the industrious and rational, and "labour was to be his title to it" (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §34, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Starting from a world given in common, labour could give people distinct titles to parcels for their private use (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §39, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). He also says that, in the beginning, labour gave a right of property wherever someone employed it on what was common (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). He adds that God, by commanding people to subdue the earth, gave authority to appropriate (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §35, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

Locke does set limits on this. Someone who let what he gathered spoil offended against the common law of nature and invaded his neighbour's share (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §37, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)). Early appropriation was also limited by labour and enjoyment, so it was impossible for a man to intrude on another's right (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). These are limits on legitimate property, not a denial of it.

detail.question: What does Mill say about the familiarity of the reasons supporting liberty of thought and expression?
detail.answer:
Mill says the grounds for liberty of thought, and for the cognate liberties of speaking and writing, are less familiar than one might expect. He notes that these liberties already form part of the political morality of countries with religious toleration and free institutions. Even so, he says the philosophical and practical grounds on which they rest are "perhaps not so familiar to the general mind, nor so thoroughly appreciated by many even of the leaders of opinion, as might have been expected" (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). He adds that the subject has been discussed for about three centuries, and he asks the indulgence of readers to whom nothing he says will be new (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 1, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)).

Mill treats one aspect of the question differently. The defence of the "liberty of the press" as a security against corrupt or tyrannical government has, he says, been "so often and so triumphantly enforced by preceding writers" that it need not be insisted on again (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). So he treats that political argument as already well established. The wider grounds he describes as less familiar.

detail.answer:
Locke says he is willing to change his mind on liberty when he finds good reason, and that he has already done so once. In the Epistle to the Reader he says that on closer inspection of how men's minds work he "found reason somewhat to alter" his earlier thoughts about what finally determines the Will in voluntary actions. He says he acknowledges this openly, and that he is more concerned to give up his own opinion than to oppose someone else's when truth appears against it (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). He describes himself as seeking truth alone, which will always be welcome to him (same passage).

In Book II, Chapter 21, §74, he calls himself "a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines" and owns some change of opinion on will, volition, liberty and necessity. He says he does not claim infallibility and would not hide his mistakes to protect his reputation. He also says he would be much obliged to anyone who could fairly clear the subject of liberty of its remaining difficulties (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 84 (edition-specific)).

In §73 he explains how one revision came about. He feared a mistake in his account, and a judicious friend suspected one without being able to show it. A stricter review then led him to a "very easy and scarce observable slip": he had put one seemingly indifferent word for another. That discovery gave him the view he presents in the second edition (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 83 (edition-specific)).

There is a qualification. Locke says his readiness to give up an opinion on the first evidence of error has not been tested by his critics. He has found no light in the printed objections against his book and no reason to change his sense on the points questioned. He suggests his meaning may be mistaken because of the subject's difficulty or because of obscurity in his own expressions (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant describes reason's logical use as the "faculty of conclusion," meaning mediate (indirect) judgement. It works by subsuming (placing) the condition of a possible judgement under the condition of a given judgement (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The process has three steps:
1. The understanding thinks a rule, the major, which says something generally under a certain condition (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
2. Judgement subsumes a cognition under the condition of that rule, which is the minor (same passage).
3. The cognition is determined by the rule's predicate, which is the conclusio. Kant says this is determined à priori by reason (same passage).

The logic is that the rule's condition is met in a particular case. So what holds generally under that condition must also hold in that case (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Kant's example runs from "All compound is changeable" and "Bodies are compound" to "Bodies are changeable." Reason thus reaches a conclusion through a series of conditions, which are the premisses (same passage).

The process can be extended. The rule can itself be treated as a conclusion, and the condition of its condition can be sought through a prosyllogism. The aim is to find for the conditioned cognition of the understanding the unconditioned, which completes its unity (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Kant adds that reason tries to bring the variety of the understanding's cognitions under the fewest possible principles, producing the highest unity (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant also distinguishes two employments of reason in moving from general to particular. If the general is certain and given, judgement need only subsume the particular under it, and the particular is necessarily determined. He calls this the demonstrative or apodeictic employment (Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). If the general is only problematical, a mere idea, then particular cases are examined to see whether they follow from the rule. If all collectable cases do, its universality is inferred. Kant calls this the hypothetical employment (same passage).

detail.question: What does Kant say about the reality of the object associated with the idea of systematic unity?
detail.answer: Kant says the object tied to the idea of systematic unity is only an idea and is not a real thing in itself. Reason cannot think systematic unity without also thinking an object for the idea. That object cannot be presented in any experience. Kant calls it "a mere idea" that is "not assumed to be a thing which is real absolutely and in itself". It is only the "problematical" (uncertain, merely supposed) foundation for the connection the mind introduces among phenomena. We treat that connection as if it came from the supposed being, but all we want is a secure basis for the systematic unity of experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). Kant makes the same point in other terms. The idea of a supreme intelligence has no immediate relation to an object, and we cannot establish its objective validity in that sense. It is a schema, and a "heuristic" rather than "ostensive" conception. It does not tell us what an object is like. It only shows how to investigate objects in experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). He therefore warns against "hypostatizing" (treating as a real thing) the principle of systematic unity and giving it an anthropomorphic determination. He calls this a perversion of reason that actually undermines the unity of nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 54 (edition-specific)). Two qualifications. First, Kant does say the idea of the systematic unity of nature must be supposed to have objective validity and necessity, in relation to the criterion of empirical truth (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)). That concerns the validity of the unity as a principle, not the real existence of the corresponding object. Second, Kant notes that it is "very natural" to assume a legislative reason corresponding to the idea, from which nature's unity would be derived (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 56 (edition-specific)). He presents this as a natural tendency, not as a proven existence. The passages given do not settle every detail of how he then limits that assumption.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the word Church (Ecclesia) "signifieth in the Books of Holy Scripture divers things" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He lists these senses:

1. A house. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's House, a Temple where Christians assemble for holy duties. Hobbes says this use is metaphorical, since it really names the congregation assembled there. It was later applied to the building itself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. A civic assembly. When not meaning a house, it means what Ecclesia meant in the Grecian Common-wealths: an assembly of citizens called forth to hear the Magistrate. Hobbes calls it a Lawfull Church if lawful authority called it, and a confused Church if tumultuous clamor did (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. The men who have a right to be of the congregation, though not actually assembled. This means the whole multitude of Christian men, however dispersed. Hobbes also lists a certain part of Christians, the Elect only (the Church Triumphant, or Church To Come), and a congregation assembled of professors of Christianity, whether their profession is true or counterfeit (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

4. One Person. Hobbes says only in the last sense (an assembled congregation) can the Church be taken as one Person able to will, command, or make laws. He defines a CHURCH as a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign, at whose command they ought to assemble (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, In What Sense The Church Is One Person Church Defined, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).
