detail.answer:
The question assumes the opposite of what the passages say. Hobbes does not argue that the sovereign should never regulate opinions and doctrines. He argues that doing so belongs to sovereignty and is the sovereign's duty. The passages give these reasons.

1. Opinions drive actions, and peace depends on governing actions. Hobbes says it is annexed to the Sovereignty to judge which opinions and doctrines are averse to peace and which conduce to it. He adds that the actions of men proceed from their opinions, so well governing opinions is well governing actions, for the sake of peace and concord (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

2. Regulating doctrine by peace does not conflict with truth. Hobbes grants that in matters of doctrine only truth should be regarded. But he says a doctrine repugnant (contrary) to peace can no more be true than peace can be against the law of nature (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He concedes that where governors have been negligent and false doctrines are widely received, contrary truths may give offence. Even so, he says a new truth never breaks the peace but only sometimes awakens war. Those who take up arms for an opinion are already in a state of war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He concludes that the sovereign should be judge of opinions, or appoint all such judges, to prevent discord and civil war (same passage).

3. Private judgments would distract the commonwealth. Hobbes rejects the doctrine that whatever a man does against his conscience is sin. He says conscience is the same as judgement and may be erroneous, and that for a subject the law is the public conscience. Otherwise the diversity of private consciences, which are only private opinions, would distract the commonwealth, and no one would obey the sovereign further than seemed good in his own eyes (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 29, Erroneous Conscience, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

4. It is a duty the sovereign must not give up. Appointing teachers and examining which doctrines are conformable or contrary to the defence, peace and good of the people is listed among the essential rights of sovereignty. Hobbes says it is against the sovereign's duty to renounce these rights, because the commonwealth would then dissolve into war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 30, Against The Duty Of A Soveraign To Relinquish Any Essentiall Right of Soveraignty Or Not To See The People Taught The Grounds Of Them, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

5. Many people think themselves wiser than the rest. Hobbes notes that among men many think themselves wiser and abler to govern the public. They strive to reform and innovate, and this brings distraction and civil war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 17, Do Neverthelesse Live In Society, Without Any Coercive Power, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Hume claim that the opposite of any matter of fact is impossible to conceive without contradiction?
detail.premise: Hume claims that the opposite of any matter of fact is impossible to conceive without contradiction.
detail.answer:
Hume's reason is that denying a matter of fact never produces a contradiction, so the denial can be conceived as clearly as the fact itself. He contrasts matters of fact with demonstrable truths. The contrary of a matter of fact "can never imply a contradiction," and the mind conceives it "with the same facility and distinctness" as the truth (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His example is that "the sun will not rise to-morrow" is as intelligible as "it will rise," and implies no more contradiction (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). If such a proposition were demonstratively false, it would imply a contradiction and could not be distinctly conceived. So we cannot demonstrate its falsehood (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Hume makes the same point about existence. The non-existence of any being is "as clear and distinct an idea as its existence," so no negation of a fact involves a contradiction (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He sets this against the sciences "properly so called," where a false proposition is confused and unintelligible. His example is that the cube root of 64 equals half of 10, which cannot be distinctly conceived. By contrast, it is perfectly conceivable that Caesar or the angel Gabriel never existed (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

A related claim is that thought is limited only by absolute contradiction. Anything never seen or heard of may still be conceived, except what implies such a contradiction (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section II, §13, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume also draws a consequence for belief. No matter of fact is believed so firmly that we cannot conceive its contrary, so belief differs from mere conception by a sentiment or feeling. His example is a billiard-ball that I can easily conceive stopping on contact, a conception that implies no contradiction (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

The passages give this as Hume's claim and illustration. They do not offer a more detailed argument for why matters of fact differ in this way.

detail.question: What does Hume suggest about the origins of widely believed extraordinary stories?
detail.answer:
Hume suggests that widely believed extraordinary stories come from ordinary features of human nature, not from real miracles. He gives several sources.

1. Pleasure in wonder. Surprise and wonder are an agreeable emotion, which gives a tendency to believe the events that cause it. Even people who cannot believe such events like to share the satisfaction second-hand and take pride in exciting others' admiration (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. Pleasure in spreading news. He compares miracle reports to rumours of marriages in country towns. The pleasure of telling and propagating interesting news spreads it. He asks whether the same passions, and stronger ones, lead people to believe and report religious miracles with great vehemence (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. Religion, vanity and self-interest. When religion joins the love of wonder, a religionist may be an enthusiast who imagines things, or may knowingly persist in a falsehood for a holy cause. Vanity and self-interest also push him. His hearers often lack the judgement to examine his evidence, so their credulity and his impudence feed each other (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

4. Plain lying, with some stories flourishing in a favourable setting. Hume says it is not strange that men lie in all ages. He says the famous lies that grew monstrous arose from beginnings like those of marvellous tales that are scorned and abandoned. Those famous lies, he says, were sown in a more proper soil (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

5. A lasting propensity, strongest among ignorant peoples. Early histories are full of prodigies. These thin out as ages grow more enlightened, which shows to Hume that it all proceeds from mankind's usual propensity towards the marvellous. Sense and learning may check this inclination at intervals, but it can never be thoroughly extirpated (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Hume's conclusion is that when such reports fly about, the natural explanation is credulity and delusion, and many such stories are detected or fade into oblivion. He therefore says we should not posit a miraculous violation of the laws of nature (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §97, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes treats a crime as a particular kind of sin. He defines a crime as "a sinne" that consists in committing, by deed or word, what the law forbids, or in omitting what the law commands. From this he concludes that every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The main difference is visibility and accusability. Merely intending to steal or kill is a sin, even if the intention never shows in word or deed, because God sees human thoughts and can charge them to a person. It is not a crime until some deed or word makes the intention apparent. Of intentions that never appear in any outward act, there is no place for human accusation (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hobbes supports this with Greek and Latin vocabulary. The Greek word translated "sin" means any swerving from the law whatsoever, while the words translated "crime" mean only the sin of which one man may accuse another. Likewise, the Latin peccatum covers every deviation from the law, while crimen means only sins that can be shown before a judge, and so not mere intentions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

A further difference is the kind of law involved. Hobbes links sin to law in general and crime to the civil law. When law ceases, sin ceases, but the law of nature is eternal, so violating covenants, ingratitude, arrogance, and acts against moral virtue never cease to be sin. When the civil law ceases, crimes cease, since only the law of nature remains. Then every man is his own judge, accused only by his conscience. In that situation a wrongful act is a sin but not a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes also gives a case where the same act changes status. If a subject refuses to obey a command that conflicts with a liberty the sovereign has granted, that is a sin. If the subject also resists a public minister carrying out the command, it becomes a crime, because the subject could have been righted on complaint without breaking the peace (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Excuses Against The Author, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

Sin is also broader than breaking a particular law. It includes any contempt of the legislator, and so can lie in the intention or purpose to transgress. Hobbes says that mere pleasure in imagining something is no sin, whereas resolving to carry out an act that tends toward it is (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant holds that human reason cannot comprehend why the moral law is unconditionally necessary, though it can grasp that this is so. Reason by its nature pushes toward a consciousness of necessity, but it can only discern the necessity of anything by supposing a condition for it. So it keeps seeking the unconditionally necessary and must assume it "without any means of making it comprehensible to itself" (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)). Kant treats this as a limit of human reason in general, not a flaw in his deduction of the supreme principle of morality. Reason cannot explain the categorical imperative's necessity by a condition such as an assumed interest, because then the law would stop being a supreme law of reason. His conclusion is that "we comprehend its incomprehensibility," which is all a philosophy that pushes its principles to the limit of human reason can fairly be asked to deliver (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)).

Related limits appear elsewhere. Kant says it is impossible for us to explain how and why the universality of the maxim as a law, that is, morality, interests us. He adds that it is certain that the law does not bind us because it interests us; it interests us because it is valid for us, since it has its source in our will as intelligences (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)). Practical reason may think itself into a world of understanding without overstepping its limits, but it may think of that world only in terms of its formal condition, the universality of maxims as laws and hence the autonomy of the will (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)). At one point he also says that if the moral law were merely presupposed in the idea of freedom, we could not prove its reality and objective necessity independently, and could give no satisfactory answer about why its validity restricts us (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). This is stated tentatively ("It seems then as if...").

The passages do not fully settle how Kant resolves that earlier worry. They do show that reason recognizes the law's authority, for example even a villain recognizes the authority of the law while transgressing it (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 19 (edition-specific)). In the Critique of Pure Reason he says he assumes pure moral laws that are absolutely imperative and therefore necessary, and that he is warranted in this by moralists and by every person's moral judgement (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages do not directly address an explicit sovereign command to break the law. They speak most closely to a related case, where the lawmaker only tacitly approves an act the law forbids. In that case, Hobbes does not fully excuse the subject. He says the case produces "two contradictory Lawes" because the will of the lawmaker is itself a law. These would "totally Excuse" only if men were bound to notice the sovereign's approval through signs other than what is expressed by his command (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). Since that condition is not met, the subject is not wholly excused. He remains guilty, but of a lesser crime than if the act were condemned by both law and lawmaker (same passage). Hobbes adds that the sovereign is "in part a cause of the transgression" because punishments attach both to breaking the law and to observing it, so he cannot reasonably put the whole crime on the offender (same passage). Hobbes frames this as a call for rulers not to countenance obliquely what they forbid directly, not as a license for disobedience (same passage).

Related passages give background. The sovereign is not subject to the civil laws, because he can repeal them whenever he pleases (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 26, And Not Subject To Civill Law, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Hobbes also treats some excuses as total, such as obeying an enemy who holds a man captive, where "such obedience is no Crime" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Totall Excuses, paragraph 25 (edition-specific)). Nothing in the passages applies that reasoning to obeying one's own sovereign's command to break the law. The passages therefore leave unanswered exactly why such a subject would be guilty before the sovereign. Hobbes's reasoning is clearest only for the tacit-approval case, where guilt is reduced but not removed.

detail.question: According to Locke, why does the bond between male and female animals sometimes last beyond mating?

top_retrieved.author: John Locke
top_retrieved.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2

detail.answer:
Locke says the bond sometimes outlasts mating because the purpose of the male–female union is "not barely procreation, but the continuation of the species". The union therefore ought to last after procreation for as long as the young need nourishment and support. They are to be sustained by their parents until they can provide for themselves (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He says the lower creatures steadily follow this rule, and he gives examples:
- Grass-eating animals: the bond ends with the act of copulation, because the mother's teat can feed the young until they can eat grass. The male has nothing to contribute (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).
- Beasts of prey: the bond lasts longer. The mother cannot easily feed herself and her numerous offspring alone, so the male's help is needed until the young can hunt for themselves (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).
- Birds: the cock and hen generally stay mates until the young can fly and fend for themselves. Locke excepts some domestic birds, where plentiful food excuses the cock from feeding the brood (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

For humans, Locke thinks the longer bond has a "chief, if not the only" reason. The woman can conceive and is commonly pregnant again before the previous child is independent, so the father stays with the same woman longer (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Where the young can fend for themselves before procreation returns, the conjugal bond dissolves of itself (Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Locke states the human explanation tentatively ("I think").

detail.answer:
Smith points to several weaknesses, and the passages describe them for particular cases rather than for every British fort. They also leave unclear which company the "committee" belongs to.

1. Weak oversight of the committee that maintains forts and garrisons. Parliament grants about £13,000 a year, and the committee must account for it each year to the cursitor baron of exchequer, with the account then laid before parliament. Smith doubts that parliament, which "gives so little attention to the application of millions," will give much to this sum. He also doubts that the baron, given his profession and education, is skilled in the proper expense of forts and garrisons (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

2. A second check is weak too. Naval captains or other officers appointed by the board of admiralty may inquire into the forts and report to that board. But the board seems to have no direct jurisdiction over the committee and no authority to correct those it inquires into. The captains are also not supposed to be deeply learned in fortification (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

3. Weak sanctions and incentives. Smith says removal from a three-year office with very small lawful emoluments seems the utmost punishment for any fault short of direct malversation or embezzlement. He argues that fear of this punishment can never force continual and careful attention to a business in which the committee-man has no other interest. As an example, the committee is accused of sending out bricks and stones from England to repair Cape Coast Castle, and the materials were said to be of bad quality (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

4. Regulated companies are poorly suited to maintaining forts. Smith says their directors have no particular interest in the prosperity of the general trade for whose sake the forts are maintained. A decline in that trade may even benefit their private trade (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). They also manage no common capital, so their only fund is casual revenue such as admission fines and corporation duties. Even with the same interest, they can seldom have the same ability to make their attention effectual (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). Smith contrasts joint-stock companies, whose directors' private interest is tied to the general trade and to the forts that defend it (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Hume say about the certainty of the science that studies the mind?
detail.answer:
Hume holds that the science of the mind is not uncertain or "chimerical" (imaginary), unless one adopts a scepticism so extreme that it would undermine all speculation and even action (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). His reasoning is that the mind clearly has distinct powers and faculties, and that there is therefore a truth and falsehood in propositions about them, which lies within human understanding (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Obvious distinctions, such as will versus understanding or imagination versus passions, are within everyone's grasp. The finer philosophical distinctions are "no less real and certain, though more difficult to be comprehended" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He also points to recent successes in these enquiries as a guide to the certainty and solidity of this branch of learning (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Hume qualifies this. The mind's operations are hard to examine, since they seem obscure when reflected upon, so even just distinguishing and classifying them (a "mental geography") is a real achievement, and the science is "by no means obvious" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that the chief obstacle in the moral or metaphysical sciences is the obscurity of ideas and ambiguity of terms, and that we may be satisfied with tracing the mind's principles through a few steps, since nature soon halts enquiries into causes and makes us acknowledge our ignorance (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §48, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). The passages do not give a fuller account of how certain particular results are.

detail.answer:
Burke raises several concerns about how the confiscated Church lands are being managed financially.

1. The fund was supposed to be free of charges, but new burdens keep being loaded onto it. He says the Assembly put a "new charge" on this fund, which was meant to show a surplus: compensation for the disbanded judicature and for suppressed offices and estates. He cannot fix the amount, but says it unquestionably comes to many French millions. A further charge is an annuity of £480,000 sterling for interest on the first assignats (paper currency issued against the lands), payable only "if they choose to keep faith" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

2. The costs of management have not been fairly stated. Burke asks whether the Assembly has ever honestly accounted for the expense of managing the lands. They are entrusted to the municipalities and a "legion of unknown under-agents" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

3. A clear, exact public account was needed and is lacking. Burke says an open statement of the property's clear value, and of the time, circumstances and place of sale, was necessary to efface the stigma attached to land-banks. It was also needed to honour the Assembly's pledge of 14 April 1790 that the lands would be freed of charges for religion, the poor and pensions (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 403 (edition-specific)). More generally, he says those who took on the role of financier were bound to show they understood the office, and to make their bank a real fund of credit as far as possible (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 401 (edition-specific)).

4. The sale plan is flawed. Burke argues that putting the whole mass of land on the market at once would depreciate land values across France and divert circulating money from trade to land. He describes the Assembly's shifting schemes, including exchanging stock for lands, and the municipalities' demand for a share, as driven by pressing public needs (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 219 (edition-specific)).

5. The payment terms favour purchasers without money. Only part of the price is paid up front and twelve years are allowed for the rest. Burke calls this a kind of gift, a project "to let in a body of purchasers without money." He expects these purchasers to pay from the rents, from the spoil of buildings, from waste in woods, and from squeezing the peasants. He notes that the rents could as well have gone to the state (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 222 (edition-specific)).

The passages give Burke's criticisms, not any actual accounting of the sums involved. He admits he cannot ascertain the amount of the new charges.

detail.question: What misconception about the meaning of 'utility' does Mill address in this paragraph?
detail.answer: In this paragraph Mill addresses the mistaken belief that "utility" means something opposed to pleasure. He calls this an "ignorant blunder" of supposing that defenders of utility use the word in a "restricted and merely colloquial sense in which utility is opposed to pleasure" (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says that writers from Epicurus to Bentham who held the theory of utility meant by it pleasure itself, together with exemption from pain. They did not mean something contrasted with pleasure. They also did not set the useful against the agreeable or the ornamental, but declared that the useful includes these among other things (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Mill notes that the same people often make the opposite charge, that utilitarianism refers everything to pleasure in its grossest form (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that the common herd, having caught only the sound of the word "utilitarian," use it to mean the rejection or neglect of pleasure, beauty, ornament or amusement. Sometimes they even use it as a compliment, as if it implied superiority to frivolity (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says this perverted use is the only one in which the word is popularly known, and the one from which the new generation are acquiring their sole notion of its meaning (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke objects to the constant talk of resistance and revolution for several connected reasons, drawn mainly from two adjacent paragraphs.

1. It turns an emergency remedy into a daily habit. He says he never liked "this continual talk of resistance and revolution, or the practice of making the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread." He argues that this makes the habit of society "dangerously valetudinary" (that is, sickly), like taking periodical doses of poison or repeated stimulants to our love of liberty (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)).

2. It wears out the spirit needed for great occasions. This habitual "distemper of remedy" relaxes and wears out, through vulgar and prostituted use, the spirit that should be exerted on great occasions. In ordinary times, he says, it has bad effects even on the cause of liberty itself (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)).

3. It encourages hypocrisy, levity, and inaction. Burke observes that many high-bred republicans soon became thorough courtiers. They left the tedious, moderate, practical resistance to others. Hypocrisy delights in sublime speculation because, never intending to go beyond it, it costs nothing. Even where levity rather than fraud is suspected, these professors find their extreme principles unfit for cases that call only for a qualified, civil and legal resistance, so in such cases they offer no resistance at all. For them it is "a war or a revolution, or it is nothing" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)).

4. It breeds contempt for public principle and bad citizenship. Finding their schemes unsuited to the world, they come to think lightly of all public principle (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)). Those who stay steady keep some change in Church or State constantly in view. Burke calls them "always bad citizens" who are indifferent to the actual state of public affairs, and who even rejoice in bad management as more propitious to revolution. They judge men and actions only by whether they advance their design of change, and they pass between violent prerogative and wild democratic ideas without regard to cause, person, or party (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 113 (edition-specific)).

5. The anniversary sermons threaten the Revolution's own legacy. He warns that such sermons, if men are not shamed out of them, will cheat many out of the principles and benefits of the Revolution they commemorate (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)).

The passages also show Burke treating some of this talk as vain discourse in which the spirit of liberty "evaporates." He thinks it worth attention mainly because it supports the scheme of "cashiering kings for misconduct" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 52 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages give Wollstonecraft's view of gallantry (polite, flattering attention to women) mainly in two places, and both are critical.

Effects on women: She says the "cold unmeaning intercourse of gallantry" has rendered many women "vain and useless". She calls it a "heartless attention to the sex" that is nonetheless reckoned manly and polite (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). She also rejects the idea that it shows real respect. She asks of men who stare insultingly at women, "Is this respect for the sex?" She contrasts "the libidinous mockery of gallantry" and "the insolent condescension of protectorship" with true personal respect, which she describes as the modest respect of humanity and fellow-feeling (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 7, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

Effects on society: She treats gallantry as a "vestige of gothic manners", a leftover of an older code. She fears it will not disappear until society is very differently organized, because it is thought so polite. She also says it prevails in the most civilized European states together with "extreme dissoluteness of morals". Her example is Portugal, where it "takes place of the most serious moral obligations." There, she says, a man is seldom assassinated in a woman's company, and a woman may be asked to pardon the rudeness of a killing and depart in peace, perhaps sprinkled with her husband's or brother's blood. She presents this as a hollow substitute for real morality (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere she says this loose, gallant behaviour shows "habitual depravity" and "weakness of mind". She concludes that it is vain to expect much public or private virtue until both men and women grow more modest (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 7, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give a fuller account of gallantry's effects beyond these points.

detail.answer:
Burke argues that the new French Constitution severs the link between the people and their representatives. In his words, there is "little, or rather no, connection between the last representative and the first constituent" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)). A member of the National Assembly is "not chosen by the people, nor accountable to them". Three elections occur before he is chosen, and two sets of magistracy stand between him and the primary assembly. This makes him, as Burke has said, "an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke says any fix would make matters worse. Letting primary electors instruct the later electors would "plunge them back into that tumult and confusion of popular election" that the graded elections were meant to avoid. Unless the people break up this gradation, Burke concludes, they do not substantially elect to the Assembly at all, and "they elect as little in appearance as reality" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke also ties this to the splitting of France into separate republics. He says the scheme tends to sever France into republics that are independent of each other, held together only by the National Assembly, which he calls in effect a congress of ambassadors from each (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 318 (edition-specific)). He contrasts this with Britain. There each representative would represent the whole and a standing government is the point of reference. In France, "the elective Assembly is the sovereign, and the sole sovereign" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 325 (edition-specific)).
